results.fact: Location of Watson Pass and where the maintained trail ends
results.correct_value: The ~4,800 ft saddle is an unnamed saddle at the wilderness boundary; the maintained trail crosses it and descends to the Watson Lakes (4,400 ft), where the scramble route leaves the trail. No source calls any point 'Watson Pass'.
results.evidence: The Forest Service trail page: second junction at 4,700 ft, left fork climbs 0.5 mi to a saddle where the trail enters the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping to the Watson Lakes at 4,400 ft. WTA: the trail to the left climbs briefly then drops down to the lakes. A 2024 trip report leaves the trail after rounding the second lake and climbs talus toward Watson. The Mountaineers route page calls it 'the saddle above Watson Lakes (~4,800 ft)', from which a boot path runs south along the ridge toward Upper Anderson Lakes (an alternative line).

results.fact: Day-by-day gain/loss vs camp and trailhead elevations
results.evidence: The day figures (2,900 up/100 down on day 1; 900 up/3,700 down on day 2) are impossible against the 4,200 ft trailhead and 5,400 ft camp, but the rules forbid re-cutting per-day figures unless the new total matches gain_ft/loss_ft, and those two columns (2,400 / 3,800) disagree with each other. Outside figures disagree too: one route page gives 2,000 ft round trip for the north-side route, a 2024 trip report about 3,000 ft. A source stating per-day or car-to-car gain for the overnight version would settle it.

results.correct_value: July-September window; earlier in it is easier on the snow (later, moats open and the glacier finger turns to ice).
results.evidence: The Mountaineers route page rates the route an alpine scramble in early season when snow-covered and a basic alpine climb in late season once the glacier surface is bare blue ice. A late-July 2024 trip report turned back from the west gully because of a large moat and snow bridge. Both support 'earlier is easier on the snow' but neither recommends June, which the seasonal guidance marks marginal; the trip-plan note now says 'earlier within July-September' instead of 'early summer'.

patches.find: Go early summer if possible - by mid-to-late summer melt-out
patches.replace: Within the July-September window, earlier is easier on the snow finger and gullies - by mid-to-late summer melt-out

results.fact: Which side of Watson the high camp is on
results.correct_value: North side (the camp sits on the north slopes, on the line from the lakes to the north-side glacier and the 5,900 ft col).
results.evidence: The Mountaineers route page brings both routes to the base of the glacier on the north side of Mount Watson (~5,700 ft) and ascends from the north side to the col. A 2024 trip report camped around 5,400 ft on the slopes beneath the peak after climbing from Watson Lakes and describes the standard approach as from the north. Neither source puts the approach or camp on the west or east side.

results.evidence: 'Start extremely early (2-3 am)' and 'depart by 3-4 am' overlap: one is when to get going, the other the latest departure. The first-ascent party's own account has them waking at 2 am and leaving camp around 3 am, which satisfies both.

Accounts genuinely disagree: one trip report reached the summit ~10 h after leaving camp and was back at camp 21 h after leaving; a 2023 report went camp to summit in 4.5 h and summit to camp in 6.5 h; the 1946 first ascent went from the 6,500 ft schrund (10:30 am) to the summit by 3:30 pm. The PUBLISHED TIMES (7 up / 5 down) sit near the fast end, the itinerary (20 h summit day) at the slow end. Settling it needs the owner to choose a representative pace, or a guide-level source giving a typical camp-to-camp time.

results.evidence: The 1946 first-ascent account says Beckey kicked steps 800 ft up a 50-degree ice couloir above the schrund. A 2023 trip report describes downclimbing roughly 800 ft of the couloir snow. The breakdown row's 50 m length was a single-pitch default.

results.correct_value: A built anchor around a stack of summit blocks, not fixed gear
results.evidence: A trip report says the first rappel was off a stack of rocks on the summit block. The row's own station and hazards text agree; only the anchor-type label said 'fixed anchor (pin/sling)'.
No outside source states a maximum cam size for this route; a 2023 report says only 'small rack (placed 2 pieces)'. A route page or report naming the largest piece would settle 2 in vs 3 in.
